{{center|The First Decade, or that of {{tooltip|Wăn Wang|Wén Wáng}}.}}
{{c|{{sc|Ode 1. The Wăn Wang.}}}}
{{dhr|0%}}
{{smaller block/s}}
{{hanging indent/s}}
{{asc|Celebrating king Wăn, dead and alive, as the founder of the dynasty of ''K''âu, showing how his virtues drew to him the favouring regard of Heaven or God, and made him a bright pattern to his descendants and their ministers.}}
 
The composition of this and the other pieces of this decade is attributed to the [[Author:Ji Dan|duke of ''K''âu]], [[w:King Wen of Zhou|king Wăn]]'s son, and was intended by him for the benefit of his nephew, the young [[w:King Cheng of Zhou|king ''Kh''ăng]]. Wăn, it must be borne in mind, was never actually king of China. He laid the foundations of the kingly power, which was established by his son [[w:King Wu of Zhou|king Wû]], and consolidated by the duke of ''K''âu. The title of king was given to him and to others by the duke, according to the view of filial piety, that has been referred to on [[Sacred Books of the East/Volume 3/The Shih/Odes of the Temple and the Altar#Duke_of_Zhou|p. 299]].
{{hanging indent/e}}
{{smaller block/e}}

{{center block/s}}

Although {{tooltip|''K''âu|Zhōu}} was an old country,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
The (favouring) appointment lighted on it recently<ref>The [[w:Ji (Zhou dynasty ancestral surname)|family of ''K''âu]], according to its traditions, was very ancient, but it did not occupy the [[w:Predynastic Zhou|territory of ''K''âu]], from which it subsequently took its name, till {{BC}} 1326; and it was not till the time of [[w:King Wen of Zhou|Wăn]] ({{BC}} 1231 to 1135) that the divine purpose concerning its supremacy in the kingdom was fully manifested.</ref>.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
